name: Leukoencephalopathy with calcifications and cysts (Labrune, SNORD118)
aliases: leukoencephalopathy with brain calcifications and cysts

clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive cerebral microangiopathy caused by variants in SNORD118, which encodes a small nucleolar RNA
The defining imaging triad is leukoencephalopathy, intracranial calcifications and parenchymal cysts, and this combination is the key to pattern recognition
Computed tomography is particularly useful for demonstrating the calcification, while MRI shows the white matter change and the cysts, which may enlarge over time and exert mass effect

Presentation varies from infancy to adulthood and includes seizures, focal neurological deficits, movement disorders, cognitive decline and features of raised intracranial pressure from expanding cysts
Unlike Coats plus (a CTC1-related disorder), Labrune syndrome is confined to the nervous system without retinal, gastrointestinal, bone marrow or systemic manifestations
Diagnosis combines the characteristic imaging triad with SNORD118 sequencing, remembering that variants affect a non-coding RNA gene and may be missed by analyses focused on protein-coding regions
Management is largely neurosurgical and supportive, with consideration of surgical drainage or resection of symptomatic enlarging cysts and control of seizures and raised pressure
reference.pathophysiology: Labrune syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in SNORD118, a gene encoding the box C/D small nucleolar RNA U8, which is involved in the processing and maturation of ribosomal RNA. Disturbed ribosomal RNA biogenesis is thought to render cerebral small blood vessels vulnerable, producing a progressive microangiopathy with vascular wall thickening, calcification and breakdown of the blood-brain barrier. The resulting chronic tissue injury generates the leukoencephalopathy, dystrophic calcification and progressively enlarging fluid-filled cysts that together define the disorder, while the disease remains restricted to the central nervous system.
additionalDifferentials: Coats plus syndrome and other CTC1-related telomere disorders
Congenital infections causing calcification (the TORCH group, including cytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis)
Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome and other interferonopathies with calcification
Primary familial brain calcification (SLC20A2 and related genes)
Cerebral neoplasm or abscess when a solitary enlarging cyst dominates
Other genetic small-vessel diseases with white matter change and calcification
additionalInvestigations: Computed tomography of the brain to define the distribution and extent of calcification
MRI to characterise leukoencephalopathy, cysts and any mass effect, with follow-up to monitor cyst growth
SNORD118 sequencing, ensuring the non-coding gene is specifically analysed
Congenital infection screen to exclude TORCH causes of calcification
Interferon signature or related testing if an interferonopathy is being considered
Neurosurgical assessment when cysts are symptomatic or enlarging
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure from an enlarging cyst requiring urgent neurosurgical review
New focal deficit or rapid neurological deterioration
Status epilepticus or poorly controlled seizures
Progressive cognitive decline with loss of independence
reference.prognosis: The course of Labrune syndrome is variable and often slowly progressive, punctuated by episodes related to cyst enlargement or seizures; outcome depends on lesion location, the rate of cyst growth and the success of neurosurgical intervention. Some patients stabilise for long periods, whereas others accumulate neurological disability over time.
pitfalls: Attributing the calcification to a congenital infection and not pursuing the genetic diagnosis
Confusing the disorder with Coats plus by failing to look for the systemic features that distinguish CTC1 disease
Missing SNORD118 variants because sequencing was targeted only at protein-coding genes
Underestimating the tendency of cysts to enlarge and cause delayed mass effect
Overlooking treatable contributors such as seizures while focusing on the imaging findings
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Neurosurgical intervention for symptomatic or enlarging cysts by fenestration, drainage or shunting to relieve mass effect
Serial CT and MRI surveillance to monitor cyst growth, calcification and white-matter change
Management of raised intracranial pressure from expanding cysts
Symptomatic treatment of movement disorders and neurorehabilitation support for cognitive and focal deficits
Neurology, neurosurgery and clinical genetics multidisciplinary care
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive SNORD118 disorder
